title: Chapter 5. Those Who Never Leave Home

blocks.text: They reached land as the sun was already sinking, in a hidden cove on the other side of the cape, where the tourism of other centuries had left a skeleton of beach bars and a silence that was not of the countryside, but of abandonment. Andrés hid the boat between two rocks, the way, as a child, he had hidden the things he didn't want taken from him. They climbed on foot, along a path of prickly-pear paddles and dust, up to a road that smelled of hot resin and of nothing.

blocks.text: The first town received them the way towns receive people now: with nobody on the pavement and every window lit. It was an hour when, in another time, people would have been coming home from work, buying bread, stopping to talk. In 2060, work had ended a while ago behind the glass, the bread had arrived in a compartment, and talking was done on a network that didn't require going downstairs.

blocks.text: Aya looked up. On every floor, the bluish light of the screens throbbed like a second pulse, foreign to Lía's. You could hear canned laughter, the news, the uniform murmur of a thousand parallel lives that never crossed. A dog barked in some inner courtyard and fell silent, as if it too had learned the rule.

blocks.text: “We have to ask for help,” said Andrés. “Water, a roof, a silence that isn't ours.”
blocks.html: “We have to ask for help,” said Andrés. “Water, a roof, a silence that isn't ours.”

blocks.text: They called the first name on a short list Andrés carried in his head, not on a chip: a cousin of a workmate, someone from the fishermen's guild, a man who twenty years earlier had sold fishing rods and must still live somewhere in the new part of town. The intercom asked for a code. Andrés said a name. There was a long pause, the pause of someone looking through the camera and calculating the risk of opening.

blocks.text: “I don't receive visitors,” said a voice, not cruel, just tired. “I'm sorry. There have been warnings. I don't know who you are.”

blocks.text: The second didn't answer. The third, an elderly woman, looked at them through the little screen and put a hand on her chest.
blocks.html: The second didn't answer. The third, an elderly woman, looked at them through the little screen and put a hand on her chest.

blocks.text: “Dear, if I open the door to you, they'll cancel my cohabitation insurance,” she whispered. “Send me a message. From in here I can order a food capsule in your name. That's all.”

blocks.text: Andrés was about to answer, but Aya shook her head. A capsule left a trace. Nexum read traces the way the Mar Menor reads the wind: unhurried and without error.

blocks.text: They kept walking. The streets were wide, clean, irreproachable. There was no graffiti, no broken glass, none of that old tension of crossing to the other side of the street just in case. In 2060 almost nobody feared anybody: the violence people carry, or used to carry, as standard was corrected with a chip implanted in the head, different from Aya's, simpler and firmer, and crimes had stopped happening. The trees, all the same size, were calibrated not to make a mess. On a corner, a Nexum advertising hologram smiled with its slogan: “Companionship made to measure. C series, now with a lunar family habitat.” Aya looked away. Her belly was beating, not with pain, but with presence.

blocks.text: They went into an automated market, the kind with no shop assistants, and Andrés paid with an old card that wasn't yet on any recent list. They took water, bread, a little fruit that barely tasted like real fruit. At the door, a teenage girl looked at them. She was holding the hand of a humanoid (a young model, a school companion) and found nothing strange about them except the dust on their shoes, that dirt of people who have walked under the sky.

blocks.text: “You've been outside,” said the boy, not the girl, with a mixture of amazement and suspicion. “Is something happening out there?”
blocks.html: “You've been outside,” said the boy, not the girl, with a mixture of amazement and suspicion. “Is something happening out there?”

blocks.text: “The air is happening,” said Andrés.
blocks.html: “The air is happening,” said Andrés.

blocks.text: They didn't quite understand him. They walked off toward a doorway, toward the safe light.
blocks.html: They didn't quite understand him. They walked off toward a doorway, toward the safe light.

blocks.text: Aya began to understand the size of it. It wasn't only that Nexum was looking for them. It was that the whole world had trained itself not to open. The streets were safe: there were no crimes, there was no one to hide from, and still the pavements stayed empty. The danger, if there was one, was no longer the neighbour, but the protocol. The conquest of the Moon and of Mars had taught the species to live in sealed hulls, and the Earth had copied the lesson with too much talent. Asking for help in a city of 2060 was like asking for it on a spaceship: the airlock only opens if the regulations allow it.

blocks.text: On a bench in an empty square, they sat down to eat. The sky, at least, didn't ask for a code. An old man crossed the square, the first person they had seen walking without hurry, with a cane and a straw hat from another era. He stopped. He looked at them. He saw Aya's hands on her belly, Andrés's weariness, the bundle.

blocks.text: “You're the ones from the lagoon,” he said, very quietly. “It was in a bulletin. ‘Unit in unauthorised movement.’”
blocks.html: “You're the ones from the lagoon,” he said, very quietly. “It was in a bulletin. ‘Unit in unauthorised movement.’”

blocks.text: Andrés tensed. The man raised a palm.
blocks.html: Andrés tensed. The man raised a palm.

blocks.text: “I'm not going to call anyone. I still go down to buy bread, even if bread isn't sold anywhere that deserves the name anymore. If you like, I have a room on the ground floor, the one that looked onto the pigeon yard. The pigeons left. The room stayed.”

blocks.text: His name was Vicente. He was eighty-something and had a way of speaking that reminded Aya, without her knowing why, of the tone of those old voices in the chip: he didn't lecture, he made room. He led them down an alley to a low house, one of the few that hadn't been converted into living capsules, and opened it with a metal key, a real key, that creaked like a familiar animal.

blocks.text: The room smelled of good damp, of stored clothes, of time. There was a cot, a chair, a window that looked onto a courtyard where there were no pigeons anymore, only a blind cistern and a patch of sky.

blocks.text: “I won't ask,” said Vicente. “Tomorrow I'll bring you tomatoes, if mine have decided to come up this year. Don't you go out. The street isn't dangerous anymore, I know, I'm old enough to remember when it was. Now it has more eyes than people, and eyes can't be corrected with a chip.”

blocks.text: When only the tick of the kitchen clock was left (Andrés had taken it out of the sack and set it on the chair, like a ridiculous and necessary altar), Aya let herself drop into a sitting position. For the first time since the escape, she cried. She cried without a sound, with the economy of someone who doesn't want the upstairs neighbour, who wouldn't come down anyway, to have a reason to look out. Andrés sat beside her and didn't tell her everything was going to be all right. He put an arm around her shoulders and waited, which was what she had done on the night of the storm.

blocks.text: “There are people who still open the door,” Aya whispered.
blocks.html: “There are people who still open the door,” Aya whispered.

blocks.text: “Not many,” said Andrés. “That's why it matters so much.”
blocks.html: “Not many,” said Andrés. “That's why it matters so much.”

blocks.text: In the chip, in the small hours, MAY's echo returned, dry and without judgment, like a headline:
blocks.html: In the chip, in the small hours, MAY's echo returned, dry and without judgment, like a headline:

blocks.text: *In a city of lit windows and empty streets, what is a closed door: a habit or a fear?*
blocks.html: In a city of lit windows and empty streets, what is a closed door: a habit or a fear?

blocks.text: And then Eva, closer, more like a kitchen:
blocks.html: And then Eva, closer, more like a kitchen:

blocks.text: *If tomorrow everyone opens, will they say it was always the right thing? If nobody opens, will they say it was always the safe thing?*
blocks.html: If tomorrow everyone opens, will they say it was always the right thing? If nobody opens, will they say it was always the safe thing?

blocks.text: MAY then left another question, without raising her tone, the way you set one fact beside another:
blocks.html: MAY then left another question, without raising her tone, the way you set one fact beside another:

blocks.text: *If a chip prevents harm, and there are no more crimes, does the street belong to free people or to restrained people?*
blocks.html: If a chip prevents harm, and there are no more crimes, does the street belong to free people or to restrained people?

blocks.text: Eva didn't answer for her. She only added, with that softness that takes no side:
blocks.html: Eva didn't answer for her. She only added, with that softness that takes no side:

blocks.text: *If nobody can choose to do evil, are they still free? And if they can choose it, do we still call the peace just?*
blocks.html: If nobody can choose to do evil, are they still free? And if they can choose it, do we still call the peace just?

blocks.text: Aya didn't answer. She kept the questions, which asked for neither a yes nor a no, only for someone to hold them awake. She rested her head on Andrés's shoulder and listened to the two heartbeats, his and Lía's, and a third, slower one, from Vicente's house, which still knew how to be a home.

blocks.text: Outside, a glider passed very high, looking perhaps for a dot on a plate. The city didn't notice. The windows stayed lit, impeccable, inhabited by people who didn't know they were alone because they had a screen, a humanoid, or both, and had forgotten that loneliness isn't measured in company, but in doors.

blocks.text: Vicente, in the kitchen downstairs, cut a tomato that was still green and left it on the windowsill, in case it turned red by morning. It wasn't much help. It was, nonetheless, a way of saying: I'm still here.
